title: The last cancellable moment
subtitle: A cancellation arrives as packing finishes.
question: Who decides which transition wins?

steps.title: Two requests, one order
steps.body: The customer requests cancellation while a packing clerk reports assembly complete. Both requests reach the authoritative Order Lifecycle state.

steps.title: Accept one state transition
steps.body: Use an atomic compare-and-set or transaction: Open -> Cancelled or Open -> Assembled. Once either succeeds, the competing transition fails. The cutoff remains assembly completion.

steps.title: Trigger payment only after assembly commits
steps.body: Only a successful assembly transition produces the expected-payment trigger. A canceled order cannot generate this trigger through a separate stale packing status.

decision: Order Lifecycle owns the authoritative state. Fulfillment submits completion; Billing reacts to committed assembly. Atomicity and reliable event delivery are engineering decisions derived from R29/R43.
failure: A design with independently writable cancellation and packing states can accept cancellation and still transfer an expected payment.
limit: This is an architecture walkthrough. It does not claim that the breakfast business backend or a concurrent database transaction has been implemented.

title: One more invoice, no new debt
subtitle: The packing clerk reprints a damaged invoice.
question: Does printing a document accidentally create a financial expectation?

steps.title: Assembly already completed
steps.body: The committed assembly transition has requested transfer of the expected-payment record with customer number, order number, euros, and due date.

steps.title: Request another numbered copy
steps.body: PrintInvoiceCopy creates a new copy number and renders the order snapshot. It does not invoke RegisterExpectedPayment.

steps.title: Keep triggers explicit
steps.body: Invoice printing and expected-payment registration may live in one component with distinct operations. Only assembly completion is a payment trigger. Deduplication of retries is an engineering choice, not an extra source requirement.

decision: Billing exposes separate document-print and payment-registration operations. Similar vocabulary does not require a shared trigger or transaction.
failure: Connecting payment registration to invoice printing would confuse R23's repeated copies with R43's assembly trigger.
limit: Payment processing remains in the existing external system. The expected payment date policy is unresolved in the source.

title: Two doors, the same rules
subtitle: The same breakfast order arrives through web or SMS.
question: Can changing a message format leave the business rules alone?

steps.title: Translate input at the edge
steps.body: The web form and SMS parser translate their inputs into the same PlaceOrder or CancelOrder request. The SMS adapter understands C/W/P syntax and message-length limits.

steps.title: Apply shared business rules
steps.body: Order Lifecycle checks customer eligibility, resolves products, applies blueprint constraints, and enforces the assembly cutoff for cancellation regardless of entry channel.

steps.title: Translate the response
steps.body: The core returns the assigned order number. The SMS adapter formats the required text response; the web adapter displays it. SMS cancellation authentication remains an explicit open question.

decision: Channels adapt input and output around the application core. They do not own duplicate ordering or cancellation policies.
failure: Separate web and SMS business implementations can enforce different cancellation or customer-eligibility rules.
limit: The SMS gateway is a proposed integration boundary. No real messages are sent and no phone number is contacted.
